name: P1 · Value Education
description: 3 of 8 topics so far (6 sets × 20 questions): Value Education – Basics; Teaching Methods of Value Education; Theories of Goodness. More topics are added to this pack as the plan goes on; re-importing only adds the new sets.

sets.name: 1 · Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics

questions.question: The word 'value' is derived from the Latin word 'valere', which means:

options.B: To be of worth, to be strong

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values are what a person or society considers worthwhile.

questions.question: Values are best described as:

options.C: Rules written only in law books
options.D: Standards or principles that people consider desirable and that guide their choices and behaviour

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: They direct what we think is good, right and important.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of values?

options.B: They are learnt through experience and socialisation
options.C: They are inherited genetically and cannot change
options.D: They can be arranged in a hierarchy of importance

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values are acquired and can change over time.

questions.question: The saying often used about value education, 'Values are caught, not taught', means that:

options.A: Pupils learn values mainly by observing the example of teachers, parents and society
options.B: Values cannot be learnt at all
options.C: Values must be memorised from books

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Hence the teacher's own conduct is very important.

questions.question: The main objective of value education is:

options.D: The all-round development of character so that the learner becomes a good person and a good citizen

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It develops moral, social, emotional and spiritual aspects of personality.

questions.question: Which committee (1959) was appointed specially to examine religious and moral instruction in educational institutions?
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It recommended moral instruction in schools.

questions.question: The Education Commission of 1964–66, which recommended education in moral, social and spiritual values, is popularly known as the:
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It was chaired by Dr D. S. Kothari.

questions.question: The University Education Commission (1948–49), which also stressed moral and spiritual values in higher education, was chaired by:
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It is known as the Radhakrishnan Commission.

questions.question: The National Policy on Education (1986) wanted value education mainly to help:

options.A: Eliminate obscurantism, religious fanaticism, violence, superstition and fatalism

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It saw value education as a force for social cohesion and national integration.

questions.question: A teacher who is always punctual, honest and fair to all pupils is teaching values mainly through:
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Pupils imitate the behaviour of admired adults.

questions.question: Which method of value education uses stories, dramatisation and discussion of moral dilemmas?
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values are drawn out of activities rather than preached.

questions.question: Values are said to be 'relative' in the sense that:

options.A: Their priority may differ between persons, cultures and situations
options.B: They are the same for everybody at all times
options.C: They can be measured in rupees
options.D: They depend on height and weight

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Universal values also exist, but the importance given to values varies.

questions.question: Which of the following is an objective of value education?

options.B: Developing respect for others and a sense of social responsibility

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Respect, responsibility and cooperation are core aims.

questions.question:
Match the commission or policy with its year:
a. University Education Commission
b. Sri Prakasa Committee
c. Kothari Commission
d. National Policy on Education

1. 1959
2. 1948–49
3. 1964–66
4. 1986
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: All of them stressed values in education.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Values influence a person's attitudes and behaviour.
II. Values once formed can never change.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values develop and can be modified with experience and education.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The family is the first school of values.
II. The school and the teacher also play a major role in developing values.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Family, school, peers, media and society all shape values.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The teacher's own behaviour is very important in value education.
Reason (R): Children learn values largely by imitating the people they admire.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values are 'caught' from models.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Value education aims only at improving examination results.
Reason (R): Value education aims at the development of character.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Its aim is character and all-round development; R is true and A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The Kothari Commission recommended education in moral, social and spiritual values.
Reason (R): The Kothari Commission was the first commission appointed after Independence.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: the University Education Commission (1948–49) came first.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Values are learnt and not inborn.
Reason (R): The word 'value' comes from the Latin 'valere'.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Both true, but the origin of the word does not explain how values are acquired.

sets.name: 2 · Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values

questions.question: The NCERT document on social, moral and spiritual values in education (1979) listed approximately how many values?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: The list of 83 values is widely quoted in value education courses.

questions.question: Values that are desirable for their own sake, as ends in themselves, are called:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Instrumental values are means to achieve other ends.

questions.question: Milton Rokeach classified values into two types:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Terminal values are desired end-states; instrumental values are modes of behaviour.

questions.question: Eduard Spranger's six types of values are theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political and:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: The Allport–Vernon–Lindzey Study of Values is based on Spranger's types.

questions.question: Enjoying music, painting and the beauty of nature reflects which kind of value?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Aesthetic values relate to beauty and art.

questions.question: Standing respectfully when the national anthem is played reflects a:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Patriotism and respect for national symbols are national values.

questions.question: Helping flood victims and taking part in community service reflect:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Social values include cooperation, service and concern for others.

questions.question: Punctuality, self-discipline and cleanliness are usually classed as:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: They relate to an individual's own conduct.

questions.question: Truth, non-violence, peace and love, accepted by people everywhere, are called:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: They are not limited to any one religion, region or culture.

questions.question: The core values mentioned in the Preamble to the Indian Constitution include:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: These are constitutional values every citizen should respect.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the core elements listed in the National Policy on Education (1986)?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Other core elements include India's freedom movement, constitutional obligations, common cultural heritage, egalitarianism, democracy and secularism.

questions.question: Returning a lost wallet with all the money to its owner shows mainly the value of:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Honesty is both a personal and a moral value.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi's life and teaching emphasised above all the values of:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Satya and ahimsa were the basis of his philosophy.

questions.question: Human values such as compassion and respect for human dignity are values that:

options.B: Apply only to one's own family
options.D: Relate to our common humanity and apply to all people

questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: They form the basis of human rights.

questions.question:
Match the value with its category:
a. Patriotism
b. Cooperation
c. Truthfulness
d. Appreciation of beauty

1. Aesthetic
2. Social
3. National
4. Moral
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Categories overlap in practice, but these are the usual classifications.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Intrinsic values are valued for their own sake.
II. Money is usually regarded as an intrinsic value.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Money is valued as a means to other ends, so it is an instrumental (extrinsic) value.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Secularism and democracy are among the values promoted by the Indian Constitution.
II. Protection of the environment is a core element of the National Policy on Education (1986).
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Both are correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Truth and non-violence are called universal values.
Reason (R): They are accepted as good in almost all cultures and religions.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Wide acceptance across cultures is what makes a value universal.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Spranger classified values into six types.
Reason (R): Spranger also listed the 83 values in the NCERT document.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: the list of 83 values comes from the NCERT document of 1979.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Social values help people live together in harmony.
Reason (R): Personal values relate to the individual's own conduct.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Both true, but R describes personal values and does not explain the role of social values.

questions.question: In the direct method of value education, values are taught:

options.A: Through planned, separate lessons or periods devoted specifically to values

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Moral instruction periods and talks are examples.

questions.question: In the indirect method of value education, values are:

options.B: Taught in a separate period only
options.D: Integrated with the teaching of school subjects and co-curricular activities

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: For example, a science lesson can bring out honesty in recording results.

questions.question: The incidental method of value education means:

options.B: Using events that occur unexpectedly in school or society as occasions to discuss values
options.C: Writing values on the blackboard every day

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: A quarrel in class or a news event can become a value lesson.

questions.question: A pupil returns a lost purse to the office and the headteacher praises this honesty in the morning assembly. This is an example of the:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: A real event is used to highlight a value.

questions.question: A history teacher discusses the sacrifices of freedom fighters while teaching the national movement. This illustrates the:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Values come through the subject lesson itself.

questions.question: A school has a weekly 'moral science' period where the teacher narrates stories and explains their morals. This is the:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It is a separate, planned period for values.

questions.question: Presenting a story with a moral problem and asking pupils what the character should do is the:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It is associated with Kohlberg's work on moral reasoning.

questions.question: In role play for value education, pupils:

options.A: Act out situations to experience different viewpoints and feelings

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It builds empathy and understanding.

questions.question: The 'value clarification' approach (Raths, Harmin and Simon) mainly helps students to:

options.B: Accept the teacher's values without thought
options.C: Become aware of their own values through choosing, prizing and acting

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It focuses on the process of valuing rather than preaching.

questions.question: Celebrating national festivals, observing Environment Day and organising a school cleanliness drive teach values through:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Such activities give practice in citizenship and cooperation.

questions.question: Community service such as visiting an old-age home mainly develops the value of:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Pupils learn through direct experience of serving others.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the limitation of relying only on the direct method?

options.A: Values may remain as information that is not practised in behaviour
options.D: It takes no time at all

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Values must be experienced and practised, not only explained.

questions.question: School assembly with prayers, thought for the day and news reading is a means of value education because it:

options.B: Gives daily, shared experiences of discipline, reflection and awareness

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It sets the tone for the school day.

questions.question:
Match the method with its example:
a. Direct method
b. Indirect method
c. Incidental method
d. Role play

1. Bringing out cooperation while teaching a group experiment in science
2. Pupils enact a scene of helping an injured person
3. Discussing a fight in the playground when it happens
4. A separate moral-education period with stories
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Schools generally combine all these methods.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. In the indirect method, values are integrated into subject teaching.
II. In the incidental method, the teacher uses events that happen by chance.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Both descriptions are correct.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Value education is effective only when it is examined through written tests.
II. Stories and discussions can be used in value education.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Values show in behaviour; written tests alone cannot measure them.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The incidental method makes value lessons meaningful.
Reason (R): It uses real situations that pupils have just experienced.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Real events make the value concrete and relevant.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Values can be developed only through a separate moral-science period.
Reason (R): Every subject and activity in school can carry values.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Because every subject and activity can carry values, A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Role play helps pupils understand others' feelings.
Reason (R): Role play requires expensive equipment.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: A is true; R is false – role play needs almost no materials.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Discussing moral dilemmas develops moral reasoning.
Reason (R): Kohlberg proposed three levels of moral development.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Both true, but Kohlberg's levels do not by themselves explain how discussion helps.

sets.name: 2 · Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers

questions.question: Mass media such as television, newspapers and the Internet influence values mainly because they:

options.D: Reach large numbers of people and present models of behaviour

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Children often imitate what they see on screen.

questions.question: A negative influence of media on children's values can be:

options.D: Exposure to violence, consumerism and stereotypes

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Guidance helps children view media critically.

questions.question: A positive use of media in value education is:

options.A: Letting pupils watch any content without guidance
options.C: Showing a documentary on environmental conservation followed by discussion

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Discussion turns viewing into learning.

questions.question: 'Media literacy' means the ability to:

options.B: Access, analyse, evaluate and create media messages critically

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: It protects children against misinformation and manipulation.

questions.question: Checking whether a message forwarded on social media is true before sharing it shows the value of:
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Fake news can cause real harm.

questions.question: Cyberbullying is best prevented in school by:

options.C: Teaching respectful online behaviour, empathy and how to report problems

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Digital citizenship is part of modern value education.

questions.question: The most important role of the teacher in value education is to:

options.A: Be a role model whose own conduct shows the values taught

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Pupils notice whether a teacher practises what they preach.

questions.question: A teacher treats all pupils equally regardless of caste, religion or gender. This models the value of:
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Equal treatment is also a constitutional value.

questions.question: Creating a classroom climate where pupils feel safe to express opinions promotes the values of:

options.B: Freedom of expression and mutual respect

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: A democratic classroom teaches democracy by practice.

questions.question: Involving parents in value education is important because:

options.A: Values learnt at school are reinforced (or weakened) at home
options.B: Values are learnt only at home

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Home and school must work together.

questions.question: The NCERT (2012) document on values in schools is titled:

options.C: Education for Values in Schools – A Framework

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: It advocates a whole-school approach to values.

questions.question: A 'whole-school approach' to value education means:

options.A: Values are reflected in the school's policies, climate, relationships and all activities
options.D: Values are taught once a year

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Everyone in the school contributes.

questions.question: A teacher who comes late regularly but lectures pupils on punctuality is likely to:

options.D: Fail to develop the value, because the example contradicts the words

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Values are caught more than they are taught.

questions.question:
Match the medium with a value-education use:
a. Newspaper
b. Film
c. Radio
d. Internet

1. Listening to an educational broadcast programme
2. A news-reading and discussion session in assembly
3. Viewing and discussing a story of courage
4. Researching a social issue online for a project
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: All media can serve value education with guidance.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Media can influence children's values both positively and negatively.
II. The teacher should help pupils evaluate media messages critically.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: That is the purpose of media literacy.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The teacher's behaviour has little effect on pupils' values.
II. Parents also shape children's values.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: The teacher is one of the strongest models for pupils.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Teachers should model the values they teach.
Reason (R): Pupils learn values largely by imitating people they respect.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Modelling is the most powerful method.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): All media content is harmful to children.
Reason (R): Media can present violence and stereotypes.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Some content is harmful, but much is educational; A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Media literacy should be part of value education today.
Reason (R): Media literacy means avoiding all use of the Internet.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: A is true; R is false – media literacy means using media critically, not avoiding it.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A democratic classroom helps develop democratic values.
Reason (R): The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Both true, but the date does not explain why a democratic classroom develops those values.

sets.name: 1 · Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism

questions.question: Something that is good in itself, valued as an end and not for anything else, has:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Happiness and virtue are common examples of intrinsic goods.

questions.question: Something that is good because it helps us get something else has:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Money is good as a means to food, shelter, education and so on.

questions.question: Which of these is usually given as an example of an external (instrumental) good?
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Its value lies in what it can buy or achieve.

questions.question: Kant held that the only thing good without any qualification is:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Opening idea of Kant's Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785).

questions.question: Hedonism is the ethical theory that:

options.C: Duty for duty's sake is the highest good

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). From Greek hēdonē, 'pleasure'.

questions.question: Psychological hedonism holds that:

options.A: By nature, people always seek pleasure and avoid pain
options.B: People ought to seek the pleasure of others

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Ethical hedonism says what people OUGHT to seek; psychological hedonism describes what they DO seek.

questions.question: The Greek philosopher associated with egoistic, sensual hedonism (the Cyrenaic school) is:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). He valued the intense pleasures of the present moment.

questions.question: Epicurus taught that the highest pleasure is:

options.C: Freedom from pain in the body and from disturbance in the mind (ataraxia)

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: He preferred simple, lasting, refined pleasures.

questions.question: Utilitarianism, a form of universalistic hedonism, judges an action right if it produces:

options.A: Obedience to rules regardless of results
options.C: The greatest pleasure for the doer only
options.D: The greatest happiness of the greatest number

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Associated with Jeremy Bentham and J. S. Mill.

questions.question: Jeremy Bentham's hedonic (felicific) calculus measures pleasures by their:

options.A: Quantity – intensity, duration, certainty, nearness, fecundity, purity and extent

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Bentham: 'quantity of pleasure being equal, pushpin is as good as poetry'.

questions.question: J. S. Mill differed from Bentham by holding that pleasures differ in:

options.B: Quality as well as quantity – higher (intellectual) pleasures are better than lower (bodily) ones

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.'

questions.question: The 'paradox of hedonism' states that:

options.A: Pleasure and pain are the same
options.C: Those who chase pleasure directly often fail to find it; it comes as a by-product of other pursuits

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Discussed by Henry Sidgwick.

questions.question: The Indian school that held 'as long as you live, live happily' (yāvat jīvet sukhaṃ jīvet) is:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). A materialist, hedonistic school.

questions.question: For Aristotle, the highest human good is:

options.B: Eudaimonia – flourishing or well-being achieved through a life of virtue

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism

sets.name: 2 · Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution

questions.question: Moral pluralism holds that:

options.A: There are many genuine moral values or duties that cannot all be reduced to a single one
options.C: There is no right or wrong
options.D: Every culture has exactly the same rules

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Monism, by contrast, reduces all value to one supreme principle.

questions.question: The philosopher who proposed several 'prima facie duties' (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, non-maleficence) is:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). A classic statement of moral pluralism (The Right and the Good, 1930).

questions.question: In moral pluralism, when two duties conflict (e.g. keeping a promise vs helping someone in danger), a person must:

options.B: Use judgement to decide which duty is weightier in that situation
options.C: Always follow the first duty learned

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Ross called the winning duty one's 'actual' duty in that case.

questions.question: The view that the single highest good is pleasure is an example of:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution

questions.question: Which of the following is a moral quality (virtue)?
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution

questions.question: Plato's four cardinal virtues are:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Each corresponds to a part of the soul or a class in the ideal state.

questions.question: Self-control, especially over desires and appetites, is called:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Aristotle placed it as the mean between excess and insensibility.

questions.question: The self-realisation (self-evolution) theory says that the highest good is:

options.D: The full development of a person's true self – intellectual, emotional and moral

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution

questions.question: Which statement best expresses self-evolution as a moral ideal?

options.B: A person grows morally by steadily developing good qualities and controlling lower impulses

options.D: A person is born perfect and cannot change

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution

questions.question: For Mahatma Gandhi, the ultimate aim of life was:

questions.question: Aristotle described a virtue as:
